lessonTitle: Vital Signs, Early Warning Scores and Escalation

blocks.text: On a post-operative ward, a patient's observations at 08:00, 12:00 and 16:00 each look 'a bit off but not bad': a slightly faster pulse every time, a blood pressure drifting down. No single set triggers an alarm. By 20:00 he is in septic shock. The warning was in the direction of travel, and nobody was reading the trend.

blocks.markdown: Patients rarely collapse without warning. In many cases there are abnormalities in basic observations for hours beforehand. An **early warning score (EWS)** turns a set of vital signs into a single number so that deterioration can be recognised early and acted on consistently. In the United Kingdom the standard system is the **National Early Warning Score 2 (NEWS2)**, developed by the Royal College of Physicians. This unit teaches how to record a complete set of observations, calculate NEWS2, follow the escalation steps, and interpret trends.

blocks.title: Early warning score
blocks.text: A **track-and-trigger** tool that assigns points to deviations from normal in routinely measured physiological parameters. The aggregate score estimates the risk of deterioration and tells staff how often to monitor and who must respond. A score supports, but never replaces, clinical judgement.

blocks.markdown:
### A full set of vital signs

NEWS2 uses **seven** parameters: **respiratory rate**, **oxygen saturation**, whether the patient is on **supplemental oxygen**, **systolic blood pressure**, **pulse rate**, **level of consciousness** (alert, or new confusion/voice/pain/unresponsive, scored together as CVPU) and **temperature**. Measure every one, every time; a missing parameter makes the score unreliable. Respiratory rate is the parameter most often estimated or omitted, yet it is often the earliest sign of deterioration, so count it over a full minute while the patient is unaware. Use correctly sized equipment, record the time, and repeat any surprising value before acting on it, unless the patient looks unwell, in which case act first.

Read each row left to right: the column heading gives the points. For temperature the columns read 3, 1, 0, 1, 2 (the table is laid out so that low values are on the left). The **aggregate score** is the sum of the seven parameter scores. Separately, a score of **3 in any single parameter** (a 'red score') is important even if the total is low.

blocks.title: Calculating a NEWS2 score
blocks.prompt: A 63-year-old man on a surgical ward has: respiratory rate 22 per minute, oxygen saturation 95% breathing air, systolic blood pressure 105 mmHg, pulse 98 per minute, alert, temperature 38.4 degrees C. Calculate the NEWS2 aggregate and state the clinical risk band.

steps.text: Oxygen saturation 95% falls in 94-95: 1 point. Breathing air: 0 points.
Systolic BP 105 falls in 101-110: 1 point. Pulse 98 falls in 91-110: 1 point.
Alert: 0 points. Temperature 38.4 falls in 38.1-39.0: 1 point.

blocks.answer: The NEWS2 aggregate is 6, a medium clinical risk requiring urgent review by a clinician competent in acute illness.

blocks.caption: The aggregate score is the sum of the seven parameter scores s_i.

blocks.markdown:
### Escalation linked to the score

NEWS2 links each band to **monitoring frequency** and **clinical response**. Local policies vary in detail, but the national framework is as follows.

blocks.caption: NEWS2 escalation framework
rows: Registered nurse decides whether to change frequency or escalate
Urgent ward-based response: registered nurse informs a doctor or clinician competent in assessing acute illness
Urgent response: review by a clinician competent in acute illness, consider critical care outreach
Emergency response: immediate assessment by a team with critical care skills and transfer to a higher level of care if needed

blocks.title: Why a trend can matter more than one score
blocks.prompt: A 57-year-old man is monitored 4-hourly. His respiratory rate is 16, saturation 97% on air, temperature 37.0 degrees C, and he is alert at every check. Systolic blood pressure and pulse are: 08:00 128 mmHg and 78 per minute; 12:00 116 and 92; 16:00 104 and 108; 20:00 96 and 118. Calculate the score at each time and interpret.

steps.text: Interpret: every score is 4 or less and no parameter scores 3, so on score alone each would be low risk. But the score has risen in each set, and a falling blood pressure with a rising pulse is the pattern of developing shock.
Action: escalate on the trend. Increase the frequency of observations, review the patient, look for causes such as bleeding or sepsis, and ask a senior for advice.

blocks.answer: The scores are 0, 1, 2 and 4: individually low risk but steadily rising, with falling blood pressure and rising pulse, so the patient should be escalated for urgent review.

blocks.title: Do not wait for the trigger
blocks.text: Never withhold escalation because the score has not yet reached the 'official' threshold. Clinical concern, a rising trend or a new confusion are all reasons to ask for help earlier.

points: NEWS2 sums scores for seven parameters: respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen, systolic blood pressure, pulse, consciousness and temperature; always measure the full set, especially respiratory rate.
Aggregate scores map to monitoring frequency and response: 0 routine, 1-4 low, a single 3 urgent ward-based response, 5-6 urgent clinician review, 7 or more emergency response.
Trends reveal deterioration relative to the patient's baseline before any single value crosses a threshold; escalate on trend and clinical concern, not only on the number.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the seven parameters scored in NEWS2?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: urine output is important clinically but is not a NEWS2 parameter.

questions.explanation: NEWS2 uses respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen, systolic blood pressure, pulse, consciousness and temperature. Urine output should still be recorded where relevant, but it does not contribute to the aggregate.

questions.stem: A patient on a medical ward has an aggregate NEWS2 of 6, with no single parameter scoring 3. Which response is most appropriate?

options.text: Urgent review by a clinician competent in acute illness, with at least hourly observations, and consideration of critical care outreach
Repeat observations in 4 hours and escalate only if the score reaches 10
Wait for the next ward round tomorrow

questions.correctOptionText: Urgent review by a clinician competent in acute illness, with at least hourly observations, and consideration of critical care outreach

distractorRationale.a: Correct: a score of 5-6 is medium risk and prompts urgent review with increased monitoring.
distractorRationale.b: 12-hourly observations apply to a score of 0.
distractorRationale.c: A threshold of 10 does not exist in the framework and delay is unsafe.
distractorRationale.d: Waiting until the next day is not an urgent response.

questions.explanation: An aggregate of 5 or 6 is medium risk and requires urgent clinical review and at least hourly monitoring. The response is graded, with outreach considered for ongoing concern.

questions.stem: A patient's aggregate NEWS2 is 3, made up entirely of a respiratory rate of 7 per minute, with all other parameters normal. How should this be managed?

options.text: As an urgent ward-based response because a single parameter scores 3, informing a clinician competent in acute illness
As low risk because the total is below 5, so routine observations continue
As an emergency requiring a cardiac arrest call in every case
As a measurement error that can be ignored

questions.correctOptionText: As an urgent ward-based response because a single parameter scores 3, informing a clinician competent in acute illness

distractorRationale.a: Correct: any single parameter scoring 3 triggers an urgent ward-based response.
distractorRationale.b: This ignores the single-parameter red score rule.
distractorRationale.c: A cardiac arrest call is for cardiac arrest, not a score of 3.
distractorRationale.d: A very low respiratory rate may be real and dangerous, so it must be rechecked and acted on.

questions.explanation: A score of 3 in a single parameter can signal serious physiological compromise even when the total is low. The framework therefore requires an urgent response and review.

questions.stem: A 76-year-old woman's NEWS2 is 1 at 06:00, 3 at 10:00, and 5 at 14:00. Her nurse is anxious but 'the score is still below 7'. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: The rising trend and the medium-risk score of 5 mean she should be escalated now for urgent review
No action is needed until the score reaches 7
The scores are unrelated because each is a separate measurement
Observations should be reduced to 12-hourly because she has been monitored enough

questions.correctOptionText: The rising trend and the medium-risk score of 5 mean she should be escalated now for urgent review

distractorRationale.a: Correct: both the trend and the band (5-6) call for urgent review.
distractorRationale.b: A score of 5 is already at the urgent clinician review level.
distractorRationale.c: Serial scores are linked and show direction of travel.
distractorRationale.d: A rising score requires more, not less, frequent monitoring.

questions.explanation: A steady rise from 1 to 3 to 5 shows progressive deterioration, and 5 is already in the medium-risk band requiring urgent clinical review. Waiting for 7 would delay recognition of a worsening patient.

questions.stem: True or false: a single normal set of observations in a patient who has been unwell is enough to show that they are not deteriorating.
questions.explanation: One set is a snapshot and can miss early deterioration or be falsely reassuring; serial observations show direction of change. A patient may also be improving or worsening relative to their own baseline despite similar absolute values.

questions.stem: A 48-year-old woman has a respiratory rate of 23 per minute, oxygen saturation 92% breathing air, systolic blood pressure 108 mmHg, pulse 112 per minute, is alert, and has a temperature of 36.4 degrees C. Using the NEWS2 table in the lesson, calculate her aggregate score (in points).
questions.explanation: Respiratory rate 23 scores 2, saturation 92% scores 2, air scores 0, systolic pressure 108 scores 1, pulse 112 scores 2, alert scores 0 and temperature 36.4 scores 0, giving 2 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 0 = 7. A score of 7 is high risk and requires an emergency response.

questions.stem: A 71-year-old man on oxygen has: respiratory rate 26 per minute, oxygen saturation 93% on supplemental oxygen, systolic blood pressure 98 mmHg, pulse 118 per minute, new confusion, and temperature 38.6 degrees C. Using the NEWS2 table in the lesson, calculate the aggregate score (in points).
questions.explanation: Respiratory rate 26 scores 3, saturation 93% scores 2, supplemental oxygen scores 2, systolic pressure 98 scores 2, pulse 118 scores 2, new confusion (CVPU) scores 3 and temperature 38.6 scores 1, so 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 15. A score of 7 or more is high risk, so this patient needs an emergency response.

questions.stem: Explain why a trend in observations is often more informative than a single set of values, using an example of a patient whose individual scores remain low.
markingGuide: A single set is a snapshot; a trend shows direction and speed of change
Compares with the patient's own baseline, since normal differs between patients
Gradual deterioration may never cross a threshold in any one set
Example such as steadily falling blood pressure with rising pulse and a score rising from 0 to 4 over several sets
Distinguishes persistent change from transient abnormality or measurement error
Therefore escalate on the trend and clinical concern, not only on the aggregate number
questions.explanation: Early deterioration is often gradual, so it can be detected by comparing sets rather than by any single threshold. A good answer links the trend to action such as more frequent monitoring and senior review.

questions.stem: Describe the escalation steps linked to rising NEWS2 scores, from 0 to 7 or more, including monitoring frequency and who should respond.
markingGuide: Score 1-4: low risk, at least 4-6 hourly, nurse decides on escalation
Single parameter scoring 3: urgent ward-based response with a clinician competent in acute illness informed
Score 5-6: medium risk, urgent review by a competent clinician, at least hourly observations, consider critical care outreach
Score 7 or more: high risk, emergency response by a team with critical care skills, continuous monitoring and consideration of transfer to higher level of care
Mentions that clinical concern can justify escalation at any score
questions.explanation: The framework ties each risk band to a response so that escalation is consistent and not dependent on individual confidence. Escalation is graded in urgency and in the seniority and skills of the responder.

questions.stem: Describe how you would record a full and reliable set of vital signs on a ward, and say what you would do if one value looked unexpectedly abnormal.
markingGuide: Measures all seven NEWS2 parameters: respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, supplemental oxygen, systolic BP, pulse, consciousness and temperature
Counts respiratory rate over a full minute, ideally without the patient noticing
Uses appropriate equipment and technique, such as correct cuff size and a good pulse oximeter signal
Records the time and values on the chart and calculates the aggregate score
Compares with previous sets to assess the trend
Rechecks an unexpected value unless the patient looks unwell, in which case acts and escalates first
questions.explanation: A reliable score needs complete, accurate observations; estimated or missing values, especially respiratory rate, can hide deterioration. Rechecking guards against error, but a sick-looking patient takes priority over a repeat measurement.
